items.title: Classification of numbers
items.body:
Every number in the syllabus sits in a nested hierarchy: **N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R**.

| Set | Symbol | Members | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Natural | N | 1, 2, 3, … | starts at 1 |
| Whole | W | 0, 1, 2, … | adds 0 |
| Integer | Z | …,−1,0,1,… | adds negatives |
| Rational | Q | p/q, q≠0 | terminating or recurring decimal |
| Irrational | — | √2, π, e | non-terminating, non-repeating |
| Real | R | Q ∪ irrationals | the number line |

**Special numbers:** prime = exactly two factors (smallest = 2, the only even prime); composite = more than two factors (smallest = 4); **1 is neither**. Co-prime pair ⇔ HCF = 1 (e.g. 8 & 15). Twin primes differ by 2 (11,13).

**Trap:** √(perfect square) is rational (√16 = 4); a non-perfect-square root is irrational. 22/7 is rational (only an approximation of π).
keyPoints: Nesting of number sets: N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R
Natural numbers start at 1; whole numbers add 0
Rational = p/q (q≠0) = terminating or recurring decimal; irrational = non-terminating non-repeating
2 is the only even prime and the smallest prime; 1 is neither prime nor composite
Co-prime numbers have HCF = 1; a non-perfect-square root is irrational
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Classification of Number System

items.title: Divisibility rules (shortcut table)
items.body:
Test divisibility without dividing:

| Divisor | Rule |
|---|---|
| 2 | last digit even (0,2,4,6,8) |
| 3 | digit sum divisible by 3 |
| 4 | last two digits divisible by 4 |
| 5 | last digit 0 or 5 |
| 6 | divisible by both 2 and 3 |
| 8 | last three digits divisible by 8 |
| 9 | digit sum divisible by 9 |
| 11 | (odd-place sum) − (even-place sum) = 0 or a multiple of 11 |

**Worked example (11):** For 62_35 divisible by 11 — from the right, (5+_+6) − (3+2) = 6 + _ must be a multiple of 11 ⇒ _ = 5, giving 62535 = 11 × 5685.

**Trap:** 6 needs BOTH the 2-test and 3-test; passing only one is not enough. For 11, count places from the unit digit.
keyPoints: Divisible by 3 ⇔ digit sum divisible by 3; by 9 ⇔ digit sum divisible by 9
Divisible by 4 ⇔ last two digits; by 8 ⇔ last three digits
Divisible by 6 ⇔ divisible by both 2 and 3
Divisible by 11 ⇔ alternating digit-sum is 0 or a multiple of 11
Count digit places from the right (unit digit = first/odd place) for the 11-test
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Divisibility Rule

items.title: Factors from prime factorisation
items.body:
Start with prime factorisation N = p^a · q^b · r^c …

- **Number of factors** = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1)…  (includes 1 and N).
- **Number of odd factors** = drop all powers of 2, then apply the same product.
- **Number of even factors** = total factors − odd factors.
- **Sum of factors** = [(p^{a+1}−1)/(p−1)] × [(q^{b+1}−1)/(q−1)] × …

**Worked example:** 360 = 2³·3²·5 ⇒ factors = 4·3·2 = **24**. For 1260 = 2²·3²·5·7, odd factors = (from 3²·5·7) 3·2·2 = **12**.

**Trap:** do NOT forget the +1 on each exponent, and do NOT include the power of 2 when counting odd factors.
keyPoints: Number of factors of N = p^a·q^b·… is (a+1)(b+1)…
Odd factors: ignore powers of 2, then take the (e+1) product
Even factors = total factors − odd factors
Sum of factors uses the geometric-series formula per prime
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Factors

items.title: Unit digit — cyclicity method
items.body:
Only the base's unit digit matters. Digits 0,1,5,6 keep the same unit digit at any power. Others cycle with period 4:

| Base ends in | Cycle | Period |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 2,4,8,6 | 4 |
| 3 | 3,9,7,1 | 4 |
| 7 | 7,9,3,1 | 4 |
| 8 | 8,4,2,6 | 4 |
| 4 | 4,6 | 2 (odd→4, even→6) |
| 9 | 9,1 | 2 (odd→9, even→1) |

**Shortcut:** take (power mod 4). Remainder 1,2,3 → that term of the cycle; remainder 0 → the 4th term.

**Worked example:** 3^47 → 47 mod 4 = 3 → 3rd term of (3,9,7,1) = **7**. For 17^23 + 24^24 → 3 + 6 = **9** (24^even ends in 6).
keyPoints: Unit digit depends only on the unit digit of the base
Digits 0,1,5,6 stay unchanged at any power
Cyclicity of 2,3,7,8 is 4; of 4 and 9 is 2
Use (power mod 4); remainder 0 means the 4th term of the cycle
Base ending in 4: odd power → 4, even power → 6
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Unit Digit

items.title: Trailing zeros (pairs of 2 and 5)
items.body:
Each trailing zero needs one 2 and one 5, since 10 = 2 × 5. Count both, take the minimum.

**In a factorial n!:** 5s are scarcer, so trailing zeros = ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + …

**Worked example:** 100! → ⌊100/5⌋ + ⌊100/25⌋ = 20 + 4 = **24** zeros.

**In a product/power:** prime-factorise each base, total the 2s and 5s, take the minimum.

**Worked example:** 15^50 × 20^40 × 25^30 → 5s = 50+40+60 = 150, 2s = 80 (from 20^40 = 2^80). min(80,150) = **80** zeros.

**Trap:** in a factorial the answer is always driven by 5s; in a product, check which of 2 or 5 is scarcer.
keyPoints: One trailing zero = one pair of (2 × 5); count both and take the minimum
Trailing zeros in n! = ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + …
100! ends in 24 zeros
In a product, prime-factorise, total the 2s and 5s, take the smaller count
In a factorial the 5-count is always the limiting factor
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Number of Zeros

items.title: HCF–LCM identity, remainders & perfect squares
items.body:
**HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers** (two numbers only). So a missing fourth quantity is found from the other three. For fractions: HCF = HCF(numerators)/LCM(denominators); LCM = LCM(numerators)/HCF(denominators).

**Remainders:** Dividend = Divisor × quotient + Remainder. If divisor d₂ divides d₁, then N mod d₂ = (given remainder) mod d₂.

*Example:* N ÷ 899 leaves 63; 899 = 29 × 31, so N ÷ 29 leaves 63 mod 29 = **5**.

**Remainder of powers (cyclicity):** list the remainders of the base's successive powers to find the cycle length, then use (exponent mod cycle-length). *Example:* 2^100 ÷ 7 → 2¹,2²,2³ leave 2,4,1 (cycle length 3); 100 mod 3 = 1 → remainder **2**.

**HCF/LCM word problems:** 'bells toll / lights blink together again' → **LCM** of the intervals; 'greatest number dividing a, b, c leaving the SAME remainder' → **HCF of the pairwise differences**; 'least number leaving remainder r with each divisor' → **LCM(divisors) + r**.

**Perfect-square unit-digit test:** a perfect square ends only in 0,1,4,5,6,9 — never 2,3,7,8. So 1298 (ends in 8) is not a perfect square, while 441 = 21² and 625 = 25² are.
keyPoints: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers (holds for exactly two numbers)
HCF of fractions = HCF(numerators) / LCM(denominators)
Dividend = Divisor × quotient + Remainder
If d₂ divides d₁, then N mod d₂ = (remainder when divided by d₁) mod d₂
Remainder of a^n by a divisor: use the cycle of power-remainders, then (exponent mod cycle length) — e.g. 2^100 ÷ 7 = 2
Word problems: bells toll together → LCM of intervals; greatest number leaving the same remainder → HCF of the differences
Perfect squares end only in 0,1,4,5,6,9 — never 2,3,7,8
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — LCM and HCF; Remainder Theorem; Perfect Square

items.title: Fractions, decimals & recurring decimals
items.body:
**Comparing/ordering fractions** — three quick methods:

1. **Decimals:** convert each to a decimal and compare (fastest for a small set).
2. **Cross-multiplication (two at a time):** a/b vs c/d ⇒ compare a·d with b·c.
3. **Common denominator:** rewrite over the LCM of denominators, then compare numerators.

*Example:* 3/5, 5/8, 7/12, 11/20 → 0.60, 0.625, 0.583, 0.55 ⇒ ascending **11/20 < 7/12 < 3/5 < 5/8**.

**Recurring decimal → fraction:**

- **Pure recurring** 0.(ab)… = (repeating block)/(as many 9s as digits). E.g. 0.363636… = 36/99 = **4/11**; 0.7̄ = 7/9.
- **Mixed recurring** 0.a(bc)… = (whole non-recurring+recurring block − non-recurring part)/(9s for recurring digits then 0s for non-recurring). E.g. 0.1(6) = (16−1)/90 = 15/90 = 1/6.

**Terminating vs recurring:** a fraction in lowest terms terminates iff its denominator has only 2s and/or 5s as prime factors.
keyPoints: Compare fractions by decimals, cross-multiplication (a·d vs b·c), or a common denominator
Pure recurring 0.(block) = block / (as many 9s as digits) — e.g. 0.(36) = 36/99 = 4/11
Mixed recurring uses 9s for recurring digits then 0s for non-recurring digits in the denominator
A fraction terminates iff its lowest-term denominator has only prime factors 2 and/or 5
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Fractions; Decimals

items.title: Counting terms in a range & factoring power-sums
items.body:
**Count of multiples of k in [a, b]** = ⌊b/k⌋ − ⌊(a−1)/k⌋.

*Example:* multiples of 15 (=LCM of 3 & 5) from 17 to 457 → ⌊457/15⌋ − ⌊16/15⌋ = 30 − 1 = **29**.

**Numbers divisible by BOTH x and y** → count multiples of LCM(x, y). Three-digit multiples of 7 = ⌊999/7⌋ − ⌊99/7⌋ = 142 − 14 = **128**.

**AP term count:** in an evenly spaced list a, a+d, …, l the number of terms n = (l − a)/d + 1.

**Prime counting in a range:** just list them — e.g. primes between 100 and 120 are 101, 103, 107, 109, 113 → **5**.

**Factoring a sum of consecutive powers:** pull out the smallest power. aᵐ + aᵐ⁺¹ + … + aᵐ⁺ᵏ = aᵐ(1 + a + a² + … + aᵏ).

*Example:* 6²⁵ + 6²⁶ + 6²⁷ + 6²⁸ = 6²⁵(1 + 6 + 36 + 216) = 6²⁵ × **259**, so 259 (=7×37) is a divisor.

**Trap:** for 'divisible by both', divide the range by the LCM, not by each number separately; and always factor a power-sum before testing divisibility.
keyPoints: Count of multiples of k in [a,b] = ⌊b/k⌋ − ⌊(a−1)/k⌋
Divisible by both x and y ⇒ count multiples of LCM(x,y)
AP term count n = (l − a)/d + 1
Sum of consecutive powers aᵐ+…+aᵐ⁺ᵏ = aᵐ(1+a+…+aᵏ)
6²⁵+6²⁶+6²⁷+6²⁸ = 6²⁵·259; primes between 100 and 120 are 5 in number
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Counting & Series of Powers
